meta.provenance: Concepts and trap structures derived from KMF/Gremlin's GRE source set; every stem, all numbers, all options, all explanations and all figures are original. No source text or artwork reproduced.

questions.question:
In the circle with center O, KM is a diameter and L is a point on the circle other than K or M. In triangle KLM, the angle at K measures a degrees and the angle at M measures b degrees.
Column A: a + b
Column B: 90

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="160" cy="130" r="90" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="70" y1="130" x2="250" y2="130" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="70" y1="130" x2="115" y2="52" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="115" y1="52" x2="250" y2="130" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="160" cy="130" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="164" y="126" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">O</text><text x="50" y="136" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">K</text><text x="256" y="136" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">M</text><text x="103" y="46" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">L</text><text x="86" y="124" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">a</text><text x="228" y="124" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">b</text></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Because KM is a diameter, the angle of triangle KLM at L is inscribed in a semicircle, and an angle inscribed in a semicircle is always a right angle. So the angle at L measures 90 degrees. The three angles of any triangle sum to 180 degrees, so a + b + 90 = 180, which forces a + b = 90 no matter where L sits on the circle. The two quantities are equal.
questions.trap: Students look at the sketch, see that L is nowhere near the top of the circle, and decide the answer must depend on where L is placed, choosing D. The position of L changes a and b individually, but the right angle at L is fixed by the diameter, so their sum is locked at 90 for every legal position.

questions.question: Quadrilateral WXYZ is inscribed in a circle. The measure of angle Y is 24 degrees less than three times the measure of angle W. What is the measure of angle W, in degrees?
questions.explanation: In a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, opposite angles are supplementary, and W and Y are opposite, so W + Y = 180. The second condition gives Y = 3W - 24. Substituting, W + 3W - 24 = 180, so 4W = 204 and W = 51. As a check, Y = 3(51) - 24 = 129, and 51 + 129 = 180.
questions.trap: Students who treat W and Y as adjacent angles, or who solve for Y instead of W, land on 129 or on the value 63 that comes from misreading 'three times' as 'three more than'. Only opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, and W and Y are the opposite pair here.

questions.question:
In the circle with center O, CD is a chord. Point E lies on the circle above CD and point H lies on the circle below CD. Segment EF has length p and is perpendicular to CD, with F on CD. Segment GH has length q and is perpendicular to CD, with G on CD. Neither EF nor GH passes through O.
Column A: the radius of the circle
Column B: (p + q)/2

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="160" cy="120" r="90" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="75" y1="150" x2="245" y2="150" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="110" y1="45" x2="110" y2="150" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="210" y1="150" x2="210" y2="195" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="110,140 120,140 120,150" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><polyline points="210,160 200,160 200,150" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="160" cy="120" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="165" y="116" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">O</text><text x="58" y="156" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">C</text><text x="250" y="156" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">D</text><text x="100" y="38" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">E</text><text x="214" y="208" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">H</text><text x="94" y="102" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">p</text><circle cx="110" cy="150" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><circle cx="210" cy="150" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="98" y="167" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">F</text><text x="216" y="140" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">G</text><text x="216" y="178" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">q</text></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Slide each of the two perpendicular segments sideways until it lies on the line through O that is perpendicular to CD. Sliding EF toward that line can only lengthen the part of it that reaches the circle, and the same is true for GH, because the longest chord perpendicular to CD is the one through the center. Stacked end to end on that central line, the two lengths would together fill at most a full diameter, so p + q is at most 2r. Since neither segment actually passes through O, at least one of the two slides strictly lengthens, so p + q is less than 2r and (p + q)/2 is less than r. Column A is greater.
questions.trap: Students add p and q, see a total that looks longer than a radius, and pick B. The comparison is with half of that total, not the total itself, and the ceiling on p + q is the diameter — a ceiling that can only be reached by a segment running straight through the center, which this figure rules out.

questions.question: Circles J, K and L are tangent to one another. The area of circle J is 1/25 of the area of circle K. The circumference of circle L is equal to the sum of the circumferences of circles J and K. If the area of circle L is 324*pi, what is the radius of circle J?
questions.explanation: Areas of circles scale as the square of the radius, so an area ratio of 1 to 25 means a radius ratio of 1 to 5: if circle J has radius j, then circle K has radius 5j. Circumference is directly proportional to radius, so the circumference condition says the radius of circle L equals j + 5j = 6j. From area 324*pi we get the radius of L as 18, since 18^2 = 324. Therefore 6j = 18 and j = 3.
questions.trap: Students carry the 1/25 straight across to the radii and set the radius of K equal to 25j, or they add the areas instead of the circumferences. Area ratios must be square-rooted before they become radius ratios, while circumference ratios transfer to radii unchanged.

questions.question: A square has sides of length 6. On each side of the square a semicircle is drawn outside the square, using that side as its diameter, and each semicircle touches the large circle shown at exactly one point. What is the total area of the four shaded regions?
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M160 40 A80 80 0 0 1 240 120 A40 40 0 0 0 200 80 A40 40 0 0 0 160 40 Z" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><path d="M240 120 A80 80 0 0 1 160 200 A40 40 0 0 0 200 160 A40 40 0 0 0 240 120 Z" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><path d="M160 200 A80 80 0 0 1 80 120 A40 40 0 0 0 120 160 A40 40 0 0 0 160 200 Z" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><path d="M80 120 A80 80 0 0 1 160 40 A40 40 0 0 0 120 80 A40 40 0 0 0 80 120 Z" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><circle cx="160" cy="120" r="80" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="120" y="80" width="80" height="80" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M120 80 A40 40 0 0 1 200 80" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M200 80 A40 40 0 0 1 200 160" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M200 160 A40 40 0 0 1 120 160" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M120 160 A40 40 0 0 1 120 80" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><text x="153" y="126" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">6</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Each semicircle has diameter 6 and so radius 3, and it bulges 3 units beyond the side it sits on. The center of the square is 3 units from each side, so the farthest point of every semicircle is 3 + 3 = 6 units from the center; that is where it touches the large circle, so the large circle has radius 6 and area 36*pi. The square and the four semicircles together cover 36 + 4(1/2)(pi)(3^2) = 36 + 18*pi, and adjacent semicircles only meet at the corners of the square, so nothing is double counted. The shaded area is 36*pi - 36 - 18*pi = 18*pi - 36.
questions.trap: Students take the radius of the large circle to be half the diagonal of the square, 3*sqrt(2), instead of noticing that the semicircles reach farther out than the corners do. Others subtract only the semicircles and forget the square itself, arriving at 18*pi.

questions.question:
A circular jogging track of uniform width is to be laid around a circular lawn whose diameter is 80 meters. The outer edge of the track must have a length between 120*pi meters and 260*pi meters. Which of the following could be the width, in meters, of the track?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: The lawn has diameter 80, so its radius, which is also the inner radius of the track, is 40. The outer edge is a circle of circumference 2*pi*R, so a circumference between 120*pi and 260*pi means 2R is between 120 and 260, giving an outer radius R between 60 and 130. The width of the track is R - 40, which therefore lies strictly between 20 and 90. Of the choices, 25, 40 and 75 fall in that range.
questions.trap: Students forget to subtract the inner radius and test the choices against 60 to 130 directly, which wrongly admits 75 and 95 and 120 while excluding 25 and 40. The width is the difference of the two radii, not the outer radius itself.

questions.question: A right circular cylindrical drum stands upright on its base. The drum has a height of 8 feet and a volume of 128*pi cubic feet. The circumference of the drum's base is k*pi feet. What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: The volume of a cylinder is the area of its base times its height, so pi*r^2*8 = 128*pi. Dividing both sides by 8*pi gives r^2 = 16, so r = 4. The circumference of the base is 2*pi*r = 8*pi, so k = 8.
questions.trap: Students divide 128 by 8 to get 16 and report that as the radius, or they stop at r = 4 and enter 4 for k. The question asks for the coefficient in the circumference, which requires the extra step of doubling the radius.

questions.question: The solid shown is built from five identical solid cubes, each with edges of length 3. Four cubes sit side by side in a row on a flat surface, and the fifth cube sits squarely on top of one of them. What is the surface area of the solid, including the face resting on the surface?
questions.explanation: Five cubes have 30 faces in all, and each face has area 3^2 = 9. The four cubes in the row meet at three joints, and each joint hides one face on each of the two cubes involved, so 6 faces disappear there. The cube on top hides one more face of its own and one on the cube beneath it, for 2 more. That leaves 30 - 6 - 2 = 22 exposed faces, so the surface area is 22 x 9 = 198.
questions.trap: Students compute 5 x 6 x 9 = 270 and stop, forgetting that glued faces are no longer surface. A second common slip is to count each joint as hiding only one face rather than two, which gives 26 exposed faces and the answer 234.

questions.question:
A rectangular solid has a volume of 84, and one of its faces has an area of 14.
Column A: the surface area of the solid
Column B: 120
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Call the face with area 14 the one with sides a and b, so ab = 14, and let c be the third edge. Then abc = 84 gives c = 6. The surface area is 2(ab + bc + ca) = 2(14 + 6(a + b)) = 28 + 12(a + b). Since ab is fixed at 14, a + b can be as small as 2*sqrt(14), about 7.48, when the face is a square, and can grow without bound as the face is made long and thin. So the surface area starts near 28 + 12(7.48) = 117.8 and rises without limit, which puts 120 squarely inside the possible range. The relationship cannot be determined.
questions.trap: Students find c = 6, choose the comfortable dimensions 2, 7 and 6, compute a surface area of 136, and answer A. Fixing the product ab does not fix the sum a + b, so a single convenient set of dimensions proves nothing here.

questions.question:
The area of a circle with radius m is greater than the area of a square with sides of length t*m, where m and t are both positive. Which of the following could be the value of t?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: The circle has area pi*m^2 and the square has area (t*m)^2 = t^2*m^2. Since m^2 is positive, the condition reduces to t^2 < pi, that is t < sqrt(pi), which is about 1.7725. Now test the choices: 1/2 and 5/4 are clearly below that; 7/4 = 1.75 and (7/4)^2 = 3.0625, which is less than pi, so it works; 9/5 = 1.8, 2, and 11/6 which is about 1.833 all exceed 1.7725 and fail.
questions.trap: Students compare t itself with pi rather than comparing t^2 with pi, which would wrongly admit every choice here since all are below 3.14. The squaring is what makes 7/4 and 9/5 land on opposite sides of the boundary despite being close together.

questions.question: A monument is a right pyramid with a square base. Every edge of the monument, both the four base edges and the four lateral edges, has length 12 meters. How many meters above the ground is the tip of the monument?
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="70" y1="190" x2="210" y2="190" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="210" y1="190" x2="250" y2="155" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="250" y1="155" x2="110" y2="155" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="110" y1="155" x2="70" y2="190" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="160" y1="50" x2="70" y2="190" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="50" x2="210" y2="190" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="50" x2="250" y2="155" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="50" x2="110" y2="155" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="160" y1="50" x2="160" y2="173" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="160,163 170,163 170,173" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="130" y="207" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">12</text><text x="192" y="118" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">12</text></svg>
questions.explanation: The height runs from the tip straight down to the center of the square base. That height, half of a base diagonal, and one lateral edge form a right triangle with the lateral edge as hypotenuse. The base is a square of side 12, so its diagonal is 12*sqrt(2) and half the diagonal is 6*sqrt(2). Then height^2 = 12^2 - (6*sqrt(2))^2 = 144 - 72 = 72, so the height is sqrt(72) = 6*sqrt(2).
questions.trap: Students drop the perpendicular to the midpoint of a base edge instead of to the center of the base. That distance is 6, and it produces sqrt(144 - 36) = 6*sqrt(3), which is the slant height of a triangular face rather than the height of the pyramid.

questions.question: A washer is made by drilling a cylindrical hole through the center of a solid right circular cylinder so that the two cylinders share the same axis. The outer cylinder has a diameter of 9 centimeters, the hole has a diameter of 5 centimeters, and the washer is 3 centimeters thick. The volume of the washer is k*pi cubic centimeters. What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: The washer is what is left after the inner cylinder is removed from the outer one, and both have the same height of 3. The outer radius is 4.5 and the inner radius is 2.5, so the cross-sectional area of the ring is pi(4.5^2 - 2.5^2) = pi(20.25 - 6.25) = 14*pi. Multiplying by the thickness 3 gives a volume of 42*pi, so k = 42.
questions.trap: Students subtract the diameters before squaring, computing pi((9 - 5)/2)^2 x 3 = 12*pi, which treats the ring as a small cylinder of radius 2. The difference of squares is not the square of the difference, so the two radii must be squared separately before subtracting.
